title: Moss and the Merry Mess
markdown:
Jagged peaks kissed the sky. Valleys lay swaddled in pine-dark sleep. Villages perched like daring nests on sheer rock, and the air carried ancient needles and the promise of snowmelt. Moss was a goblin of lists and schedules, a creature of calloused fingers and patched tunics, and he treated the annual Snowmelt Festival as a problem that could be solved if everyone would please stick to the plan.

The festival marked the mountain paths opening again: sun after long winter, routes for travellers and traders finally clear. Moss tapped a grubby scroll.

“The main tent needs stronger supports. The feast requires exactly three hundred plump pickled grubs. The music must start at half-past sundown. Simple. Efficient. Entirely manageable.”

A flutter of anxious energy preceded the Snowmelt Festival Committee, whose heads seemed permanently misplaced in forgotten lore. Elder Bramble, a gnome whose white beard still trailed wisps of frost, puffed out his chest.

“Ah, Moss, my industrious friend! We’ve heard whispers of your grand pronouncements!”

Moss blinked. “Pronouncements? I was detailing the plumbing for the refreshment stands so they wouldn’t freeze solid. A rather crucial matter.”

“Precisely!” chirped Willowisp, a sprite whose iridescent wings hummed. “Plumbing! The eldest sprites know the river spirits imbue the waters with luck. We must craft a ceremonial basin of moonstone and silver!”

Moss’s sigh sounded like wind in a hollow log. “I just need the pipes not to burst. No spirits. Engineering.”

A stout dwarf stroked his braided beard. “Three hundred grubs? Most auspicious. Sacred cycles of the moon. We must gather them under the Harvest Moon!”

“That’s a good round number for stew,” Moss said, feeling his plans fray. “Quantity. Appetites. Not celestial bodies.”

Their interpretations grew grander with each sensible suggestion. Reinforced supports became a magical barrier woven from moonlight and dragon’s breath to ward off legendary shadow beasts. Half-past sundown became a signal for the Sun-Singer, a mythical creature said to usher in eternal summer with a celestial song.

Moss tried, once more, to read the scroll aloud as if words might stay ordinary if spoken slowly. The committee heard a liturgy. Willowisp sketched a moonstone basin in the frost. The dwarf began a hymn about grub-cycles that had never existed. Elder Bramble, who meant well with the force of a small avalanche, proposed a procession around the tent poles before anyone had set the poles.

They were debating the dimensions of a dragon-sized ceremonial drum for this entirely non-existent singer when the sky split with a whoosh of magnificent, slightly clumsy flight.

Flicker landed in a gust that ruffled every beard and a shower of sparks that briefly lit astonished faces. His scales were brilliant emerald. His wings threw shifting shadows. His eyes were molten gold, and his ego was still under construction. He smelled of hot stone and unearned applause.

“Fear not, mortals!” he boomed, a rumble that shook the pines. “Your humble servant Flicker has arrived to witness—and perhaps grace—this most momentous occasion!”

He attempted a dramatic puff of smoke. It came out as a startled squeak and singed the edge of Elder Bramble’s esteemed hat.

“The Sun-Singer!” Willowisp shrieked. “He has come! Moss, your foresight is unparalleled! Prepare the ritual welcoming!”

Moss buried his face in his hands. “He isn’t the Sun-Singer. He’s a young dragon trying to make an entrance. And he’s burning hats.”

Flicker preened. He liked spectacle, though he was still practising the art of not setting things alight when startled. He nudged a loose rock down a slope with a satisfying clatter.

“Is this part of the welcoming ritual?” he roared. “The offering of geological destabilization? A traditional mountain greeting, perhaps?”

Pounce, Moss’s stoat, had not been watching the dragon. He had been watching the tent poles. While the committee collected rare glowing mosses and enchanted stones for a barrier against beasts that were not attending, the actual holes in the ground had gone neglected. Pounce scampered to Moss, chattering, and nudged a sturdy fallen pine branch toward the pre-drilled sockets. Then he darted to a neglected pile of lumber from Moss’s original plans and indicated, with determined grunts, that ordinary wood could be cut and fitted.

Moss followed the stoat’s gaze. “You mean these mundane pieces, properly aligned, can hold the tent without magic?”

Pounce’s whiskers twitched. Affirmative.

“And the river spirits?” Moss glanced at the committee arranging glow-worms into a spiritual conduit. “We can use drainage.”

Pounce nodded so hard his small body vibrated.

Before Moss called anyone to work, he did one unscheduled thing. He sat on a sun-warmed rock at the path’s edge and watched meltwater find the old stone channel, drop by clear drop. Pounce sat beside him, a warm comma of fur against Moss’s boot. Flicker, briefly forgotten, nosed a pine cone and did not set it on fire. The committee’s voices went distant. Snowmelt ticked. A banner, already hung too early, lifted and fell like a lung. Far down the valley a trader’s bell sounded, the first of the season, ordinary as a kettle. Moss counted ten drops. He counted ten more. The pine smell came and went with the breeze. The mountain did not require a Sun-Singer for any of them.

Then he stood.

“Everyone,” he called, voice cutting the fantastical chatter. “The legends are inspiring. The festival needs structure. Pounce and I have a more grounded approach.”

He set three tasks and refused to dress them as miracles. No one was asked to bow. No one was asked to fetch dragon’s breath. Pounce supervised the lumber with the air of a clerk who had been right all along.

First, the tent: a team cut and fitted the lumber, and the main canvas stood with the unromantic strength of good joinery.

Second, the water: a simple collection and redirection system managed the thaw without moonstone, silver, or an argument with river spirits.

Third, the banners: Flicker, eager to be more than sparks, was persuaded to fan them with his wings, a cooling breeze instead of a celestial song.

The festival succeeded by a blend of practicality and unexpected charm. The tent did not fall. Children ran under the eaves and came out counting pickled grubs on their fingers, which was as close as anyone came to a lunar cycle. The feast was plentiful. The refreshment pipes, unenchanted and unburst, poured water that tasted of stone and thaw. The music began at half-past sundown, as planned, and was spirited enough that nobody asked it to usher in eternal summer. Villagers danced. A trader sold the first spring thread. Frost-silvered roofs took the moon. Flicker’s breeze kept the banners honest without singeing another hat.

Flicker watched from a respectful distance. He had not been the Sun-Singer. He had been useful. The small determined goblin had shown him that grand pronouncements were not always the point.

As the bonfire sank and dawn softened the east, Flicker turned to Moss. “This place has a certain charm. It isn’t all grand pronouncements and dramatic exits.”

Moss, exhausted and pleased, offered a tired smile. “It’s just home.”

Flicker dipped his scaled head. “Then perhaps I’ll stay a while. Not as the Sun-Singer. As the official cloud-herder. Or the occasional dramatic arrival, when absolutely necessary. For emergencies.”

Pounce curled at Moss’s feet and made a sound as quiet as leaves. Moss rolled the scroll, now stained with stew and useful. Elder Bramble patted his singed hat as if it had survived a legend and discovered it preferred being a hat. The dwarf admitted, after a second helping of grubs, that three hundred had been a cooking number after all. Willowisp’s glow-worms, relieved of spiritual duty, simply glowed. The pines kept their own counsel. The paths were open. The stew was stew. Flicker’s true shape, which had never been a myth, settled into the village the way meltwater settles into a channel: not as a prophecy, as a useful season.
characters: Moss (list-keeping goblin of the snowmelt villages), Pounce (quiet-wise stoat), Flicker (young dragon still learning how dramatic to be)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
author: StoryGen Community
